title: Chapter 43 – The Salt Road
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

The Narrows are beautiful in spring, exactly as Mu said they would be.

Jian lies on the ridge above them with his cheek against cold slate and counts what is wrong with the beauty. The cliff on the left is streaked with wet black and hung with new green. The stream on the right is loud with melt. Between the two runs the Salt Road, a shelf of packed clay six paces wide and four hundred paces long, with a drop to the water on one side and a wall on the other and no room for a cart to turn. Wild cherry has bloomed along the lip of the gorge. White petals ride the current in long lazy lines.

It is a perfect place to kill a cart. It is also, Jian thinks, a perfect place to kill the people who come to kill it, if the people who come are in a hurry and the people who wait are patient.

He has been lying here since before dawn. Pebble is under his chest, a small warm weight curled so tight that her ridges press into his ribs. What she feels comes up through his skin as a low steady hum of attention.

Far, she says, without words. Cold things. Four. Smell-people are two.

Two of them are hounds, or one is a hound and one is something else. He has learned to read her like weather.

Far below, at the western mouth of the Narrows, the cart is rolling in.

* * *

It is a good cart. Hu built it in four nights with one good hand, and it looks like a month's wages. Under the tarpaulin lie sixty ingots of spirit-iron. Forty are slag, plated with a skin of real metal. Twenty are real. A man who sees nothing but lead will know it, Hu said. Give him gold on top and he will not dig.

The cart is drawn by a pair of oxen. Beside the near ox walks a man with a spear.

Captain Lin Mao is fifty-one, short, deep-chested and bald, with a beard the color of steel and a face that has been squinting into weather for forty years. He wears the clan's leather cuirass over a patched blue shirt. At his hip hangs a straight sword in a worn sheath. He is a Qi Refining fifth-stage, a four-element root, no genius, and he has been captain of the Green Pine guard for twenty-two years. He taught half the hill's children to hold a spear. He taught Jian, at six, how to count his steps along a wall so that he would never be lost in the dark.

Behind him walk six guards. Jian knows each of them by name, and does not let himself say any.

They are not supposed to be here. Wenyuan pulled the caravan guards three days ago. The Patriarch told the whole clan so, in the hall, with his hands on the table and his eyes on no one. Only the usual cart, he said, only the usual escort. No more. If this goes as we fear, I want them to see a small, tired, ordinary thing, and think it cheap.

It was Mao who stood up.

"Then I'll take it," he said. "Eight years the Narrows, Patriarch. I know every stone. If it's to be a decoy it had better be one that looks like it believes itself."

Wenyuan looked at him for a long time. "You understand what I am asking."

"I understand what you are not asking." The captain's seamed face did not change. "I've a daughter, a granddaughter, and a pension I never earned. Let me earn it."

That was three nights ago. Jian has not slept well since.

* * *

He watches the cart roll into the Narrows and counts, because counting is what he does.

Three hundred paces to the east mouth. Cart at walking pace, call it four hundred breaths. Ridge to road, forty paces straight down, thirty-two across. Beyond fifteen, the drum cannot reach me.

Hu says the drum is a pitch that finds the water in the bone, and cannot reach past fifteen paces. Jian is seventh stage, barely. He does not intend to find out how barely.

The plan is a plain one. It is Wenyuan's and Hu's and Mother's, and Jian has made small, careful changes. The cart goes in. The hunters, who must be somewhere close, close the road at the east mouth, where the shelf narrows and the cliff comes right to the water. Then Wenyuan's rockfall talisman, a Yellow-grade, medium tier, drawn on three nights of no sleep and pasted to the underside of an overhang four hundred paces up the gorge, will bring the cliff down behind them. The Narrows will be shut at both ends. The hunters will be inside it, with nothing to do but fight a thin line of tired guards on a shelf six paces wide.

Then Jian's work begins.

Pebble.

Here.

When the drum speaks, tell me where it is.

Where, she says doubtfully. Where is... where. Cold place in the air. I will find the cold place.

"Good enough," Jian whispers, and puts his cheek back on the slate.

* * *

They come out of the east mouth at the sound of the first bell.

It is not a real bell. It is a hoof on a stone, a slow clop, and then another, and then a dozen, out of the glare of the morning. Four figures walk out onto the shelf in a loose line, without any hurry, without any cover, like men strolling to a market. Tally in the center, huge and soft in his hooded leather, the drum riding on his belly. The Drip Sisters at his flanks in rust-colored cloaks. And a little behind, a short brown man with a broken nose and a gaunt gray hound.

The cart stops. Lin Mao raises one hand and the guards halt, and nobody draws.

"Well met," says the captain, in a perfectly ordinary voice. "Tolls are at the bridge, friends. This is clan road."

"Is it," says Mei Lian, smiling.

Neither sister has so much as moved a hand, and yet Jian, forty paces above, feels his skin crawl. It is the thread. The sisters' chains are wound on their forearms, and between the two women, from wrist to wrist, runs a hair-fine line of red that he can see only because Pebble has shown him where to look. It pulses. It makes a slow, soft, sick, living shimmer in the morning light.

Linked, Pebble tells him. They are one thing. Cut one, the other bleeds.

Good to know.

"You are carrying iron," Mei Ru says. "Spirit-iron, we hear. Sixty ingots. We would like to buy it."

"It's not for sale."

"It is a very generous price."

"It's a very bad morning," says Lin Mao, "for a man to be told what he can buy."

Mei Lian laughs. It is a pleasant laugh, bright and light, and then she makes a small gesture with two fingers, almost lazy, and the chains on both women's arms uncoil as if they had been waiting.

Mao has time to say one word. It is the word the guards have been taught to say.

"Now."

* * *

Three things happen in the same breath.

The first is the talisman. Four hundred paces up the gorge a gray slip beneath an overhang flares white, and the east wall of the Narrows lets go with a grinding roar. Boulders pour down in a brown avalanche. The road behind the hunters vanishes under forty tons of rock.

The second is the drum.

Bone Tally has not moved. He is standing with his thumbs on the skin, and as the cliff falls he lifts both hands together and brings them down.

There is no sound.

That is what Jian will remember. He is forty paces up a ridge, with his mouth open, and he hears nothing. The avalanche is silent. The stream is silent. The wind is silent. For the space of one heartbeat the whole gorge is an empty bell, and then it rings, a single vast flat note, low as a cough in a cathedral, and every guard on the shelf drops where he stands.

They do not fall. They collapse. Their knees go and their spears go and their hands go to their ears, and the blood comes out between their fingers in thin red threads. One guard vomits. One screams, soundlessly. One lies on his side with his eyes rolled back and his whole body shaking like a fish.

Jian feels the edge of it. It is a cold hum in the roots of his teeth, a dull ache in every bone of his jaw, a pressure behind his eyes. He bites down on it. Pebble, under his chest, goes rigid and gives a thin, frightened whistle, and he puts one hand on her back and holds on.

It is a pitch. It finds the water in the bone. He has, he finds, been repeating it to himself like a prayer.

The third thing is Lin Mao.

He is on one knee. His ears are bleeding. His face is the color of paper. He has dropped his spear, and his left hand is pressed to the side of his head, and his right is closed around the hilt of his sword, and he is getting up.

It takes him five breaths. Jian counts every one.

You are a fifth-stage. You cannot stand in the drum.

He stands.

"Close up!" Mao says. It is a shout. It is a ruined shout, wet and cracked, but it carries, and three of his men lift their heads. "Close up, to me! The cart! Behind the cart!"

"Why is he standing," says Mei Ru, in a tone of mild interest.

"Stubborn old thing." Mei Lian lifts her arm. The chain snaps out. "Kill him."

* * *

Jian is moving by then.

He has not decided to. His body has simply begun, the way a hand pulls from a flame. He drops over the lip of the ridge and into the shadow of a ledge twenty paces down, small and quiet in his gray cloak, with the Still Water Veil settled over him like a breath held. The ledge is thirty-five paces from the shelf. That is outside the drum, by Hu's count.

He has the Seven Seam Needles in a roll against his chest. He takes three and threads them with Qi.

Below him, the hook strikes.

It hits Mao's shield. It is a round wooden shield banded in iron, the old guard's pattern, and the hook goes through it as if it were bark. Mao drives his sword into the shield's face and wrenches. The chain pulls taut. For a moment the captain and the elder sister stand locked on either end of a black line, and then Mei Ru's hook, from the other side, takes him through the thigh.

He does not go down.

"I count," says Mao, to no one, "eleven breaths."

He is talking to the guards. They are on their feet now, three of them, then four, shaking and white. He is telling them how long they have to hold the shelf. Jian knows it. He knows, as the captain's voice cracks and the second hook is drawn back, that Lin Mao has already done this sum, in his head, three nights ago, on his own, and that he has accepted the total.

Eleven breaths. Jian lifts his hand.

Pebble.

Cold place, she says. The big man's chest. Wet, stuck. Like a drum.

Show me where the shell is thin.

Through the bond, something opens. It is not seeing, not exactly. It is the way he felt the scouts' shell in the forest, a map of tension and slack, a web of small gaps in a dense hard fabric. It is Pebble's whole body sorting the world into door and wall.

Bone Tally's Qi shell is very thick. It rolls off him in heavy gray layers, a cloak woven from years of discipline. But a drum must be held, and a drummer must lift his arms, and when a man lifts his arms the shell at the join of the shoulder splits, and in the pale gray fabric a thread-thin seam opens, a hand's width below the right armpit.

There.

There, she agrees.

Thirty-five paces. The needle will fly, if he lets it. It will go across that distance on a thread of his Qi, steady and straight, as it went for the scout. He has done it thirty times, on a straw target, in the granary, with his eyes shut.

He has never done it with a man's life on the end.

I do not need to be sure, he tells himself. I only need to be exact.

Mao has taken a second hook, in the ribs this time. He staggers and turns, and as he turns he swings the sword with his whole body into the nearest sister's chain, and the blade goes through two links. The black chain parts. Mei Lian cries out in a high sharp voice, and a thread of blood sprays from the severed link, and on her sister's wrist the matching line goes slack.

"Old fool," Mei Lian says.

Tally lifts his hands for the second beat.

Jian lets the needle go.

* * *

It makes no sound.

It is the thinnest of the seven, a spirit-iron sliver the length of a finger, and it goes across thirty-five paces of morning light so fast that even Jian, who has thrown it, cannot see where it is until it is gone. It threads the gap below Tally's armpit like a sewing needle through a buttonhole. It goes in at an angle. It goes up, as the guide of the thread directs, through lung and through the soft arch under the heart, and the point comes to rest, quivering, in the curve of the sternum.

Bone Tally's thumbs stop on the drum.

He looks down. He looks, with the faint mild curiosity of a man who has found a spot on his shirt, at the small bright thing that has appeared on the left side of his chest. He tries to speak. A bubble of red rises at the corner of his mouth, and the only voice that comes is the thin, cracked whisper that nobody has heard in eleven years.

"Oh," he says, to himself. "Oh. That is quick."

He sits down. The drum rolls out of his arms and falls off the edge of the shelf and into the stream, and goes spinning away downriver on the current, red spirals bobbing in the white water.

Then he is dead, and the pressure behind Jian's eyes is gone, and the whole gorge breathes out.

* * *

It lasts one heartbeat.

The sisters turn, both together, with the same sharp quick motion, and look up the cliff.

They felt it, Jian thinks. Not me. The needle. The thread. The Qi line from his hand to the needle is still faintly lit, and the shorter of the two women, Mei Ru, is looking straight up it like a hound on a scent.

"The boy," says Mei Ru.

She flings her chain.

It does not reach him. It cannot; thirty-five paces is far, even for a hook. But it does not have to. The hook strikes the rock above the ledge, a full body-length over his head, and the rock cracks. A slab the size of a table comes loose and slides toward him down the cliff in a spray of grit.

He throws himself flat. The slab misses his head by a hand and hits the ledge's lip with a sound like a bell, and the lip goes. He is falling.

It is not a long fall. Eight feet, perhaps ten. He hits a shelf of wet clay and rolls, and his shoulder goes into a rock, and something in his ribs makes a small, sharp, definite noise. The wind goes out of him. The Veil tears off him like a rag and is gone. For a moment he lies on his back at the lip of the shelf, in the open, and sees the blue strip of sky, very high, and the faces of the two women, very near.

"Little boy," says Mei Lian, smiling.

She has lost a chain, but she has another, and it is already moving.

Pebble, he thinks. Wall.

Wall, says Pebble, and the cliff opens.

He does not understand it. He will not, for a long time. He is lying against a face of black rock, and the black rock has a seam in it that was not there a breath ago, a hair-thin, silver gap, running from the clay to the sky. The hook, coming down, strikes the stone where his chest was. It is not there. He is not there. The seam has taken him, and he is through, tumbling sideways into a cold dry dark that smells of iron and rain, and his own heart is the only sound in the world.

It lasts three breaths. Then the dark spits him out onto a shelf of gravel fifteen paces down the gorge, behind the cart.

Pebble is on his shoulder. She is shaking all over. He can feel the cold of her through his cloak, and under the cold, a tight little knot of effort that is already beginning to fray.

Tired, she says. Tired, tired. Not again. Not for a while.

"Not again," he agrees, in a voice he does not recognize. "Thank you."

Behind the cart, the fight is still going.

* * *

Mother is there, in a gray cloak by the near wheel, the Still Water Veil on her so completely that his eye slides off her twice. A short thin knife in each hand, green with water Qi, moving in the narrow space between cart and cliff. She is a fourth-stage. Mei Lian is an eighth.

"Behind the wheel," Mother says, without looking at him. "Jian." He goes.

He sees it only in fragments between the spokes. Mei Lian's chain whipping high and low. Mother's knives not parrying but flicking, a hair's breadth, turning a hook from the neck to the shoulder. It is a fight for time, and she spends every second like gold.

And Wenqing is on the cliff above them. He has seen that too, in one lucky flash. His second uncle's wife's brother, a thin quiet herbalist with ink on his sleeve and a Sha-Edge pruning knife in his fist, has come down the broken rock on a rope. He drops without a sound. He lands on Mei Lian's back.

The knife goes in under her right shoulder blade and out through her collarbone.

She makes a small, surprised noise, and then another, and then she turns her head, slowly, and looks at the thin quiet man behind her with an expression of the most profound irritation. "You are pruning me," she says.

"Yes," says Wenqing, white-faced. "I'm so sorry."

Then she falls, and the chain on her arm goes slack, and across the shelf her sister screams.

It is not a scream of grief. It is a scream like a kettle, high and thin and ripped, and it goes on and on. The red line between their wrists is pulsing wildly now, thickening, turning black. Jian has seen what a blood link does when one end is cut. He does not want to see it again.

Mei Ru has gone to her knees. She has her hand clamped over her mouth, and from between her fingers a thin, dark thread of blood is coming, and she is looking at him.

"Boy," she says. It is very quiet. "You will pay for that."

Then, with a motion so fast that he never sees it begin, she tears the whole chain from her arm and flings it at the ground, and the world goes red.

* * *

It is not an explosion. It is a mist, hot and rust-colored, spreading across the shelf in one breath, smelling of old pennies. The guards cough. Jian puts his sleeve to his face and his eyes burn. A Drip's last card, boiled blood to cover a retreat.

When it clears, Mei Ru is gone, and so are Shan and the hound, and her sister's body with them. Only a long red smear remains on the clay.

And across the shelf, at the foot of the cart, Lin Mao is lying with his sword in his hand.

* * *

He is still breathing when Jian reaches him.

He has been put on his back by someone. Wenshi, probably, Jian's uncle, who has come down off the cliff behind the rockfall with a bloody sleeve and a broken wrist and a face like a hatchet. He is kneeling beside the captain with his good hand pressed to a wound in the old man's side. It is a bad wound. It has gone in below the ribs and out the back, and the shield and the cuirass between them have not helped.

"Don't move him," Wenshi is saying, in a flat, hard voice. "Don't. Mao. I have a bandage. I have a pill. Stay still."

"Eleven," says Lin Mao.

"What?"

"Eleven breaths." The captain's face is slack and bluish, and his bald head gleams with sweat, but his steel-colored beard is neat, and his eyes are very clear. He turns his head, with some effort, and looks straight at Jian. "I said eleven. Did we do eleven?"

Jian does not know. He did not count. He had meant to. He looks at the man and the answer will not come, and the lie that rises to his mouth tastes like bile.

"Twelve," he says.

Mao smiles.

"That's a good count," he says. "Always had a good count, you. Six years old. Wouldn't be lost in the dark." His hand moves a little on the clay. "My Lian-er. You'll tell her I held the road."

"I will."

"And the... pension." The faint smile deepens. "I never did earn it. Funny."

"Mao." Wenshi is shaking. "Mao, damn you, be quiet."

"Quiet," says the captain, kindly. "Yes. All right."

He closes his eyes. His chest rises once, and falls. It does not rise again.

For a long moment nobody in the whole length of the Narrows says a word. The stream goes on running. The cherry petals go on floating down the black water, white as the first snow, and the sun comes round the shoulder of the cliff and lights up the dead man's beard.

Then Wenshi bends, very slowly, and closes the captain's eyes with two fingers, and lays his head back on the clay.

* * *

The rest is work.

Four guards are dead, two more deaf, a third will not stop shaking. Mother has Wenqing by the shoulders, speaking to him low until he stops trembling. Wenshi does not leave the captain's side.

Jian walks down the shelf alone.

He knows where he is going. He has known since the needle left his fingers. At the foot of the east wall, where the rockfall has not yet filled the road, a huge pale shape lies sprawled on its side with its hood fallen back, and the wet red smear that was a pair of lips has already begun to stiffen. Bone Tally's eyes are open. They are blue, a child's blue, and they look up at the strip of sky with a strange mild wonder, as though he has just heard a piece of music he did not expect.

He is the first I killed face to face, Jian thinks. The scouts were a forest and a wire. Ke Tian was a rafter. This one I saw. He takes the needle from the chest, wipes it on the dead man's sleeve, and puts it back in the roll.

I am not sorry. He killed four of ours. It is a true sentence. He turns it over like a coin, and it gets no lighter.

* * *

The satchel is on Tally's left hip.

It is a plain affair of brown hide, stitched at the seams with red cord, the size of a man's two hands. A fat, cheerful wooden toggle holds it shut. He opens it with two fingers, in the shade of the cart wheel, with his back to everyone, and looks in.

There are eleven items inside. A tin of salve. A dried tongue. A string of knuckle beads. A tiny knife. Four slips of yellow paper, tied in a bundle. A vial of red powder. Two glass bottles stoppered with wax. Last, wrapped in black silk, a flat package the size of his palm.

Scan.

```
[ARK-7 — SCAN]
Object: Satchel, brown hide (non-spatial; ordinary)
Contents: 11 items
Notable:
- Recipe slips x4 (Yellow grade, medium tier)
1. Marrow Wash pill — Grade 2. Rinses channel residue,
widens Qi pathways by a small margin. Raises the next
breakthrough chance by ~4%. Brewing time 3 days.
2. Needle Ward talisman — Yellow, medium tier. Deflects
thin piercing weapons for 1 minute. One use.
3. Blood Seal pill — Grade 2. Stops bleeding from a
non-vital wound within 5 breaths. Not for internal use.
4. Salt-Bone Powder (reagent recipe)
- Vial: Red powder (Drip marrow salt; toxic)
- Bottles x2: Marrow Wash pill, ready (3 each)
- Black-silk package: spirit-iron needle case, empty
Estimated value: 140 low spirit stones.
```

He closes the satchel and sits very still.

Medium tier. It is the thing Wenyuan said they needed. Recipes a clan of four hundred can brew in a granary, with Hu's pill furnace and Mother's careful hands, and sell at the Willow Ford market for a hundred and forty stones a season. It will pay the tribute. It will keep the hill alive for a year.

It was bought with a man's life.

Everything has a cost, the interface said once. He understood it then as a statement about the world. He understands it now as a bill.

```
[ARK-7 — NOTICE]
Recipe slips: 4. Separation of non-living mixtures: 4 CE per slip. Current CE: 170. Proceed?
```

Not here, not with all of them watching. He refuses the panel, and it fades from the corner of his eye.

* * *

Wenyuan comes at noon.

He has walked the whole eleven miles, on foot, in his plain gray robe, with his sleeves rolled back and a stick in his right hand. He looks, for the first time in Jian's memory, old. The lines at the corners of his mouth have gone very deep. He stops at the end of the shelf and takes in the cart, the bodies, the blood, the stretcher.

He walks to Mao, and kneels, and stays there a long time.

When he rises he says nothing to the guards. He goes among them, one at a time, and touches each man on the shoulder, and speaks a few words close to his ear. Then he walks to the wheel where Jian is sitting, with his arms around his knees, and lowers himself onto the clay beside him.

"You are hurt."

"A rib. It's cracked. Mother has seen it."

"Yes." The Patriarch looks at the stream. "I will tell his daughter myself. Mu will know by tonight, Jian. The sister who ran will tell him of a seamwalker and a boy who throws needles. Stay close to the hill for a month."

"Yes, Father."

"And do not do that again. Wenshi saw you go into the stone." The dark sharp eyes rest on him. "I will not ask what it was. Only understand that when a boy of ten walks through a wall, there are persons who will pay a great deal to find out how."

"It was Pebble."

"A very small animal, who will grow. Yes. That is the problem." He rises. "Come. They are putting Mao on the cart. Walk beside him."

* * *

They bring him home at dusk.

It is a long slow procession up the Salt Road, past the cherry trees, with the whole clan streaming down from the hill to meet it. Lanterns. The old schoolmaster, hat in hand. A girl of nineteen in white, with her baby in her arms, who walks out into the dust and stands with a face like stone.

Jian walks beside the cart with his hand on the rail. He does not look at the girl.

Pebble is under his collar. She has not said a word since noon. He can feel her breathing, a thin, quick, dreamy flutter, and under it, very faint, something he cannot quite name. It is the feeling of a creature that has done a great thing and does not know why it hurts.

Sad, she says at last, small and puzzled. Is the big man sleeping?

No, he says, because she will find out. He's gone. He's not coming back.

A long pause. Somewhere ahead a woman begins the first line of a dirge.

I do not know his name, she says. But I will remember the smell.

He puts his hand over the lump of her under his collar. At the top of the hill the gate of Green Pine stands open, hung with white cloth, and the first stars are coming out above the roofs, hard and small and cold.

In the satchel at his hip, four recipes lie wrapped in a dead man's silk. They are worth a hundred and forty stones.

He walks the last hundred paces with his head up and his eyes dry, and does not let himself count them.
